title: BoGrape: Bayesian optimization over graphs with shortest-path encoded
one_liner: To find the best graph structure with expensive measurements, encode the candidate graphs as mathematical constraints and search them systematically instead of guessing randomly.
lead: When you want the best molecule or sensor placement but testing is expensive, Bayesian optimization helps: build a model of what works, then use math to pick the next thing to test, because a smart pick reduces the total tests needed. But existing methods struggle with finding the best graph structure (the connections between nodes). BoGrape solves this by encoding graphs as constraints in an optimization problem, so you can search the space of all connected graphs systematically instead of guessing randomly.

problem.h2: Finding the best graph is slow and haphazard
paras: Many real problems are graph problems: designing molecules (which atoms to connect?), placing sensors in a network, arranging supply chains. The goal is to find the graph structure that works best. Testing each candidate is expensive (hours in a lab, money in a trial), so you want to test as few as possible.

Bayesian optimization is a standard trick for expensive search: fit a model to what you have tested, use it to guess where the best graph might be, test that one, and repeat. But there is a catch: existing methods either assume the graph structure is fixed and you are only tweaking the features of its nodes, or they search randomly. Neither lets you systematically explore the space of different graph structures with real constraints built in (like requiring a connected graph, or molecules that are chemically valid).

callout.html: No method lets you do Bayesian optimization over the space of all possible graph structures with real constraints, so you fall back to random search or heuristics.

steps.text: Train a Gaussian process (a statistical model that guesses function values and confidence) on the graphs you have tested so far.
Each possible graph becomes a set of yes-or-no variables and mathematical equations that describe its structure (connectivity, shortest paths, node labels).

Formulate a mixed-integer program (MIP): maximize the acquisition function (expected gain) over all graphs that satisfy the encoding constraints plus problem-specific constraints (e.g., must be a molecule, must connect nodes A and B).

steps.b: Solve it with a standard MIP solver
steps.text: An off-the-shelf solver (like Gurobi) finds the graph that balances exploring uncertain regions and exploiting known good ones.
Evaluate the winning graph, add the result to your data, retrain the model, and solve the MIP again.

paras: The paper changes how you pick the next graph to test. Instead of guessing randomly or using heuristics, it formulates the choice as a mathematical optimization problem you can solve exactly (or very well). This turns graph-space search into a discrete optimization task that commercial solvers are designed to handle.
object.object: Acquisition function search (from random/heuristic to exact MIP)

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Expected gain from testing a new graph
hidden.name: Expected improvement in your best result
paras: Bayesian optimization works by balancing exploration (testing graphs you are unsure about) and exploitation (testing graphs you think will be good). To do this, it scores each candidate graph by a quantity called the acquisition function: roughly, it is the expected gain if you test that graph next. Graphs with higher acquisition scores are more likely to improve your overall best result, because the acquisition function is specifically designed to pick graphs that either look very good according to the model or reduce the most uncertainty—both of which lead to better outcomes faster.

BoGrape estimates this acquisition score for every graph that satisfies the constraints, by using the statistical model (the Gaussian process) to guess both the predicted performance and how uncertain that guess is. A graph gets a high score if the model predicts it could be very good, or if the model is very uncertain (so testing it reduces confusion).

heat.caption: Hotter graphs have higher expected gain from testing. Dark borders show top candidates.

reads.html: Some graphs are worth testing because they might be good. Others are worth testing because they are so uncertain you could learn a lot. BoGrape scores both kinds.

The acquisition function (e.g., LCB, EI, PES) quantifies the expected value of information from testing a candidate, and BoGrape computes it by evaluating the model's prediction (mean) and confidence (variance) for each encoded graph candidate.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: turning search into a solvable puzzle
paras: The core insight is that the space of all connected graphs can be represented as a set of linear and integer constraints. Specifically, if you think of shortest paths as decision variables (yes, this path of length k appears in the graph or no, it does not), then the rules for a valid connected graph become a system of mathematical equations. Once you have this encoding, you can ask a mixed-integer programming solver: among all graphs satisfying these constraints and the real-world constraints (like chemical validity), which one maximizes the expected gain?

Why does this work? First, it lets you explore systematically: the MIP solver does not guess; it searches the constraint space intelligently. Second, it respects real constraints: you can add equations that forbid invalid graphs or enforce problem-specific requirements (e.g., 'atoms must not be too close'). Third, it reuses graph kernels: the Gaussian process model relies on a shortest-path kernel, which is a standard way to measure similarity between graphs. The acquisition function is then evaluated using the model's predictions and confidence levels. The MIP solver takes the acquisition score for each candidate graph and finds the one that looks most promising.
In other words: instead of asking 'guess which graph to test next,' you ask 'solve this math problem to find it.' A mature optimization engine can solve it better than guessing.

stages.s: Graphs tested so far + their scores

Encode all connected graphs as MIP constraints
Solve: maximize acquisition subject to graph constraints

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose you have tested 3 molecules and your Gaussian process model predicts: graph G1 has score 0.7 with high confidence (variance 0.05); graph G2 has score 0.65 with high uncertainty (variance 0.3); graph G3 has score 0.6 with high uncertainty (variance 0.4).
Expected improvement EI considers: G1 is good but certain (small gain); G2 is okay but uncertain (medium gain); G3 is poor but very uncertain (could be big gain if true).

The MIP solver evaluates EI for all valid candidate graphs. Say G100 is chemically valid, satisfies all constraints, and has EI=0.25. The solver finds the graph with highest EI, say G_star with EI=0.3.
You test G_star next, measure its actual score, add it to your data, retrain the model, and solve the MIP again.

math.note: The acquisition function balances exploiting high-predicted-score graphs and exploring uncertain regions; the MIP solver does this balance globally over the constraint-encoded graph space.

charts.title: Random search
charts.note: Random sampling is slow to find the best graph.

charts.title: BoGrape
charts.note: Systematic optimization finds better graphs with fewer tests, because the MIP solver narrows the search to high-value regions instead of wasting tests on unlikely candidates; this gain holds even with real molecular design problems with chemical constraints built in.

items.b: The MIP solver is slow on large graphs.
items.html: Encoding very large graphs (hundreds of nodes) as MIP constraints creates a huge problem that solvers may take too long to solve. Practical use is best on smaller graphs (tens of nodes) or when you can decompose the problem.

If problem-specific constraints (e.g., chemical validity rules) are wrong or incomplete, the solver may pick graphs that look good mathematically but are invalid in reality. The constraints must truly capture your problem.

BoGrape uses shortest-path graph kernels. If the shortest paths do not capture the important structure of your problem, the Gaussian process model will misguide the solver. The method is not magic; it depends on a good kernel.

items.b: Done right: start with small problems.
items.html: Test the method on small synthetic benchmarks first to verify the encoding and constraints are correct. Verify that the solver actually finds valid graphs. Then move to real problems with realistic constraints and budgets.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph optimization problem: define a function that maps small graphs to scores (e.g., count the number of edge-disjoint paths, or sum of node features weighted by connectivity). Implement BoGrape and a baseline (random search, or a simple greedy heuristic). Run both for a fixed budget (e.g., 20 function evaluations), and plot the best score found over time. The demo should show BoGrape finding better graphs faster than baselines, because it uses the model to pick high-value candidates instead of guessing, and it should show that the constraints are being respected (e.g., all tested graphs are connected), because the MIP encoding enforces them automatically.
demo.closing: The demo proves that systematic optimization (MIP-based search) beats random guessing, and that the constraint encoding actually works (no invalid graphs are proposed).
